analysis.one_liner: Gives Supreme Court justices 18-year terms with a new seat opening every two years.
analysis.headline: The bill never got a hearing or a vote: it sat in the House Judiciary Committee from August 2021 until the Congress ended, and no Republican signed on as a cosponsor.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would replace lifetime Supreme Court appointments with 18-year terms, with one seat opening every two years. Justices past 18 years would move to senior status but could still fill temporary vacancies, and if the Senate sat on a nominee for 120 days, the nominee would take the seat anyway. It was referred to the House Judiciary Committee and never advanced.
analysis.who_benefits: Ordinary citizens get a Court whose makeup changes on a predictable schedule instead of turning on the luck of when a justice dies, retires, or chooses to time a departure around a friendly president. Every future president gets one confirmed seat per two-year cycle rather than a jackpot that can hand a party a decade of influence from one unexpected vacancy. The public also gains when Senate delay tactics can't leave a seat open indefinitely.

how_it_helps.text: Sets staggered 18-year terms: the President nominates one justice every two years, and after 18 years of service a justice moves to retired status.
Ends the lottery of vacancies: rather than openings depending on deaths and retirements, the number and timing of seats would be fixed and predictable.
Keeps vacancies covered: the most recently retired justice would temporarily fill any seat that opens up before a successor is confirmed, so the Court keeps nine members.
Curbs Senate stalling: if the Senate does not vote on a nominee within 120 days, the nominee is seated without its confirmation.

analysis.who_pays: Future justices give up lifetime tenure. Senators lose their ability to leave a nomination open indefinitely as a delay tactic. Sitting justices lose nothing: the bill exempts anyone already on the Court from the term limit and the new nine-member panel.

drawbacks.text: The bill grandfathers every justice already on the Court: none would be counted toward the nine-member panel or required to step back, so the current Court's composition would be unchanged and the effects would phase in only over many years.

Many constitutional scholars argue Congress cannot set Supreme Court terms by statute, because Article III of the Constitution says federal judges hold their offices 'during good Behaviour', which has long been read as life tenure; a serious version of this reform would likely require a constitutional amendment.

The 120-day automatic seating rule strips the Senate of real deliberation on a nominee and hands whoever controls the White House a guaranteed seat every two years with no backstop if the Senate has genuine objections.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The core idea — predictable, staggered terms instead of lifetime appointments decided by the timing of deaths and retirements — is a serious response to a real problem: a single vacancy can now shift the law on major questions for a generation. The bill's honest weaknesses are that it changes nothing for the current Court for a very long time, that it may not be constitutional as written, and that its automatic-seating provision trades one kind of hardball (Senate stalling) for another (a guaranteed seat for any president). A well-designed version would probably require a constitutional amendment and more careful treatment of the Senate's confirmation role.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was referred to the House Judiciary Committee, later sent to a subcommittee, and never received a hearing, a committee vote, or a floor vote before the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. Ro Khanna introduced the bill on August 31, 2021, joined by Reps. Don Beyer, Barbara Lee, and Rashida Tlaib.
It was referred to the House Committee on the Judiciary the same day.
Seventeen House Democrats, all Democrats and no Republicans, signed on as cosponsors.
On November 1, 2022, near the end of the Congress, it was referred to the Subcommittee on Courts, Intellectual Property, and the Internet.
No hearing, markup, or vote ever followed, and the bill expired when the 117th Congress ended on January 3, 2023.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Sitting Supreme Court justices keep their lifetime seats untouched, senators keep the leverage to delay or bury nominees indefinitely, and the status quo around how the Court's makeup gets decided carries on.

sides.party_line_note: All 17 cosponsors were House Democrats; no Republican supported the bill, and it never advanced past referral in a Democratic-controlled House.

industries.note: The bill exempts every justice appointed before its enactment from the term limit and from the nine-member decision panel, locking in the existing Court's composition and life tenure. Their interest in keeping lifetime, unaccountable seats runs against the public's interest in a Court whose membership changes on a schedule.

The 120-day rule would take away the Senate's ability to leave a Supreme Court seat open indefinitely by refusing to act on a nominee, a lever that has been used by both parties to shape the Court. That leverage serves the parties in power more than ordinary people.

The bill guarantees each president one Court seat per two-year cycle, ending the windfall of an unexpected vacancy but also handing a predictable seat to a president the Senate may not get to scrutinize if it stalls past 120 days.
